replies.author: @MapsideStoriesHQ
replies.text: North American railways have the same clearance problem, often expressed using AAR clearance plates such as Plate B or C. It is about the permitted height and width of the vehicle or load, including fitting through tunnels and beneath bridges, not just the platform gap. Two railways can share a track gauge without accommodating the same-sized trains.

comments.text: 15:50 Space in stations isn’t the problem; it’s the very idea of having to go through customs to catch a train that’s the problem. The advantage of the train is that you can arrive at the station five minutes before departure and leave the station five minutes after arriving. For a journey from Paris to Amsterdam (520 km), I can leave the centre of Paris and be in the centre of Amsterdam in 3 hours and 10 minutes. That’s impossible by plane. It already takes 45 minutes for security checks at the departure airport, then another 45 minutes for checks on departure. If we introduce checks at stations, then we’re removing the advantage of travelling by train. It’s important to realise that the time lost in security checks is the same time it would take a Eurostar to continue from Brussels to Frankfurt or Amsterdam, or from Paris to Lyon or Strasbourg. That’s why the Eurostar is underused.
